newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Bank MFK says no plans to sell steel stake.
newsitem.headline: Russian Bank MFK says no plans to sell steel stake.

text.p: Russian Bank MFK (ICFI) said it would welcome the participation of a Western bank in a public auction of 15 percent of Russia's Novolipetsk steelmaker.
But it repeated it had no plans to announce such an auction in the near future.

ICFI, which is associated with powerful Uneximbank (Oneksimbank in Russian), holds the stake as part of a 1995 loans-for-shares scheme where banks gave the government credits in return for custody of shares in major Russian firms.
ICFI received the stake in AO Novolipetsky Metallurgichesky Kombinat (NLMK), Russia's largest steel mill, in return for a $31 million credit to the government.

Under the terms of the 1995 programme, the stakes must be sold in a commercial investment tender after the loan's expiry, and a Western bank last week put in a bid to buy the Novolipetsk shares for $96 million.

A copy of the letter obtained by Reuters from the U.S. law firm handling the case, Mayer Brown & Platt's, said its client, the Trade Finance Bank and Trust Limited, could transfer funds immediately and called for a well-publicised public auction.
But ICFI said it was not ready to sell the shares yet.
"The loan expired on September 1, 1996, but so far we haven't decided to announce any kind of auction," ICFI press secretary Oleg Sapozhnikov said.
"Naturally a decision will be taken. When the auction takes place they are welcome to take part."
The loans for shares scheme was widely criticised as stakes often went to the very companies organising the loan tenders for the government.

A 51 percent stake in oil company Sibneft, held under the loans for shares scheme by Neftyanaya Finansovaya Kompaniya, was recently auctioned off to little-known company, Finansovaya Neftyanaya Korporatsiya, at barely above starting price.
The firm was said to have links to the bank who handled financial transactions under the tender conditions.
Sapozhnikov said uncertainty over shareholders rights at the Novolipetsk mill was contributing to the delay in announcing an auction.
"We cannot determine the investment value (of the stake) until the rights of the shareholders are protected," he said.

Bank MFK, along with fellow minority Novolipetsk steel mill shareholders Renaissance Capital and Cambridge Capital Management, won a court battle over investor rights with plant management last month.
But Renaissance Capital said on Tuesday it had filed a new complaint with the regional prosecutor.
